cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: So, Finn, I’ve done as much as I can for our project on theatre programmes. How’s your research coming along?

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: OK, Maya.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: I didn’t know theatre programmes are called playbills in the USA till I started looking into the topic.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: Even though I struggled to find many useful websites, I’m glad we picked this subject.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: No one else on the course is doing the same as us, although it is one of the research areas of the module convener.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: That might actually put some people off.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: I suppose so. Anyway I hadn’t realised there are actually companies specialising in creating theatre programmes

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Yes they are quite common nowadays.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Contrary to what many people think, theatres don’t hire people to do the programmes.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: In fact, companies buy the rights to publish programmes on the theatre’s behalf and then make their money selling advertising space within the programme booklet.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: It must be easier for theatres to do it that way.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Yes.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: I remember reading something about programmes in early British theatre. It said that the cast was always very important.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Yeah, audiences were very familiar with leading actors and big names would draw huge crowds.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: But I hadn’t realised that if the programme named a famous actor, that’s who the public expected to perform.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: And if that didn’t happen, people accused the theatre of breaking their agreement with the audience.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: They would demand refunds and if they didn’t get them, there were riots.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Outrageous! That’d never happen now.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: No, people are too polite, even when they’re disappointed if the star of the show misses a performance.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: We should definitely include that information about early audiences in our project.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: I also think it’s important to mention that lots of ordinary people at that time were illiterate, so theatre programmes were of limited value in advertising plays.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: When a company of actors arrived in a town, they’d parade around the streets in their costumes, beating drums and announcing their upcoming performances.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: Interesting. I couldn’t imagine that happening now either.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: There’s also an interesting comparison to make between 18th and 19th century programmes.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: Wasn’t it in the 19th century that theatre programmes started to resemble programs today

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Yes and unlike programs from the 18th century they always used colour

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: And there was a greater variety of designs. But personally I think 18th century programmes were superior because they told the theatregoers so many things, including about the actors.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: And about the writer, the plot and sometimes the history of the play.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: That’s right. What should we say about theatre programmes in the 20th century?

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: I reckon the most important thing is the dramatic change they underwent during World War II.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: When the government imposed restrictions on the use of paper.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Yeah, but that was only in the UK. In the USA, programmes, or rather playbills, continued to be published in the same format.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: While here in the UK, programmes became merely a single sheet of paper folded to create four pages for text.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: What I don’t really get is that after the war they didn’t go back to being more than one sheet or change in any way for over 25 years.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: I know there were paper shortages after the war, but only for five or ten years.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: Strange.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: I got some pictures of programmes we could include on the slides for our presentation.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: I found a couple too Maya. Let go through and see what we think

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Um oh this is an old one for a play called Ruey Blass

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: Never heard of that. But the programme looks very decorative.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Good enough to put in a frame on the wall. The images are just beautiful. Finn, what did you find?

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: I’ve got some pages from a programme for Man of La Mancha.

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: I thought this was a good programme to show, not because of the pictures, but because it contains articles written by members of the theatre company, so we can learn how the production was created and the thoughts and feelings of the cast.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Good.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: I’ve got a copy of a programme that’s now in a museum.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: It’s for The Tragedy of Jane Shore and it’s said to be the earliest surviving document to have been printed on Australia’s first printing press

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: Fantastic!

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: Another programme to talk about is for The Sailors Festival.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: It comes from the British Library’s digitised collection of programmes that was started a few years ago.

cues.speaker: MAYA
cues.text: It already comprises over 200,000 programmes which is amazing!

cues.speaker: FINN
cues.text: Huh. Wish I’d known about it while I was doing my research.
